questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Distinguishing troubadour from trouvère
questions.learningObjective: Identify the linguistic origin of a troubadour
questions.stem: Ticket #101 asks which language a troubadour composed in; choose the option that fits the historical record.

options.text: A troubadour composed primarily in Old French, the language of northern France.
A troubadour composed primarily in Occitan, the language of southern France.
A troubadour composed in Latin, the language of the medieval church.
options.misconception: confuses secular courtly song with sacred liturgy

options.text: A troubadour composed in Italian, the language of later madrigalists.
options.misconception: projects later practice onto earlier era

questions.explanation: A troubadour was a poet-composer of southern France who wrote in Occitan. The trouvère was the northern French counterpart writing in Old French, so option A describes the wrong group.
questions.hint: Think southern France versus northern France.

questions.topic: A courtly genre and its subject
questions.learningObjective: Name the central subject of courtly love song

stimulus.body: A ticket notes that courtly love songs dwell on longing, service, and idealized devotion. The patron asks which subject dominates the genre.

questions.stem: Ticket #102 surveys a courtly love song corpus; which subject dominates the genre according to the note?
questions.explanation: The dominant subject is courtly love itself, expressed through longing and idealized devotion. Other topics appear only as framing devices, so the count of primary subjects is one.
questions.hint: Count the primary subject, not the framing topics.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Counting the refrains across the formes fixe
questions.stem: Ticket #103 asks how many times the refrain returns in a standard rondeau of the formes fixe.

answer.exemplar: A standard rondeau returns its refrain three times across the full form, with the opening line reappearing as a half-refrain near the end, so the refrain is heard three times in full and once in part.

questions.explanation: The rondeau refrain returns in full at the opening, middle, and close, with a half-refrain before the final refrain. Thus the refrain is heard three full times and once in part.
questions.hint: Count full returns plus the half-refrain.

questions.topic: Comparing the metres of a basse danse and its saltarello
questions.learningObjective: Compare metres of basse danse and saltarello
questions.stem: Ticket #104 notes a basse danse in 6/4 and its paired saltarello in 3/4; how many basse-danse beats fit in two saltarello measures?
questions.explanation: Two saltarello measures of 3/4 give 6 quarter beats, and a 6/4 basse danse measure holds 6 quarter beats, so one basse-danse measure equals two saltarello measures; hence 4 basse-danse beats fit across the two saltarello measures counted as half-notes.
questions.hint: Convert both to quarter-note beats first.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: What a sign in mensural notation means
questions.stem: Ticket #105 shows a circle with a dot in mensural notation; what does that sign indicate?

options.text: It indicates perfect tempus, a triple division of the breve.
It indicates imperfect tempus, a duple division of the breve.
It indicates a change to minor prolation, a duple subdivision.
It indicates a rest of one breve in the mensural score.
options.misconception: confuses a mensuration sign with a rest symbol

questions.explanation: A full circle indicates perfect tempus with triple division of the breve. The dotted circle variant still marks perfect tempus, while a semicircle marks imperfect tempus.
questions.hint: Circle means perfect; semicircle means imperfect.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: The length of a maxima in semibreves
questions.stem: Ticket #106 asks how many semibreves equal one maxima in perfect (triple) mensuration.
questions.explanation: In perfect mensuration a maxima equals three breves, and each breve equals two semibreves, giving six semibreves. The tempting answer of four assumes imperfect mensuration.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: What a temperament trades away
questions.stem: Ticket #107 asks what a musical temperament necessarily trades away in exchange for usability.

options.text: It trades away melody in favor of harmonic complexity.
It trades away rhythm in favor of simpler melodic lines.
options.misconception: confuses pitch tuning with rhythmic structure

options.text: It trades away pure intervals in favor of a closed, usable system.
It trades away loudness in favor of softer dynamics.

questions.explanation: A temperament adjusts pure intervals so that music can modulate and close the circle of fifths. The cost is that formerly pure intervals become slightly impure.

questions.topic: Comparing a pure fifth with an equal-tempered fifth
questions.stem: Ticket #148 computes the equal-tempered fifth size as seven semitones of 100 cents.
questions.explanation: Seven semitones at 100 cents each equals 700 cents. This is the equal-tempered fifth, 2 cents narrower than the pure fifth.

questions.topic: Distinguishing troubadour from trouvère
questions.stem: Ticket #149 distinguishes troubadour from trouvère by their composing languages.

answer.exemplar: A troubadour composed in Occitan in southern France, whereas a trouvère composed in Old French in northern France.

questions.explanation: Language and region distinguish them: Occitan in the south for troubadours, Old French in the north for trouvères.

questions.topic: A courtly genre and its subject

stimulus.body: A ticket classifies a song praising an unattainable lady as courtly love lyric. The reviewer asks how many genres in the note are courtly love songs.

questions.stem: Ticket #150 asks how many genres in that note are courtly love songs.
questions.explanation: Only the courtly love song genre fits, so the count is one. The other genres named are epic, sacred, or dance.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Counting the refrains across the formes fixe
questions.stem: Ticket #151 counts refrains in a rondeau; how many full refrains occur?

options.text: Two full refrains, plus a half-refrain.
Four full refrains, plus a half-refrain.
Three full refrains, plus a half-refrain.
One full refrain, repeated as a half-refrain.

questions.explanation: A rondeau has three full refrain returns plus a half-refrain. Two undercounts and four overcounts.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Comparing the metres of a basse danse and its saltarello

stimulus.body: A ticket compares a basse danse measure of 6 quarter beats with a saltarello measure of 3 quarter beats. The reviewer asks the difference in beats.

questions.stem: Ticket #152 asks the beat difference between the two measures.
questions.explanation: Six quarter beats minus three quarter beats equals three. The basse danse measure is longer by three beats.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: What a sign in mensural notation means
questions.stem: Ticket #153 asks what a full circle in mensural notation indicates.

answer.exemplar: A full circle in mensural notation indicates perfect tempus, meaning the breve divides into three semibreves.

questions.explanation: The full circle signals perfect tempus with triple division of the breve. A semicircle signals imperfect tempus.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: The length of a maxima in semibreves
questions.stem: Ticket #154 computes semibreves in an imperfect-mensuration maxima: two breves times two semibreves per breve.

options.text: Eight semibreves, four breves of two each.
Six semibreves, three breves of two each.
Three semibreves, one breve of three.
Four semibreves, two breves of two each.

questions.explanation: Two breves times two semibreves per breve equals four semibreves. Six would be perfect mensuration.

questions.stem: Ticket #155 asks how many temperaments that note compares.
questions.explanation: The note compares two temperaments: meantone and equal temperament. The count is two.

questions.stem: Ticket #156 asks for the cent size of an equal-tempered perfect fifth.

answer.exemplar: An equal-tempered perfect fifth measures exactly 700 cents, seven equal semitones, 2 cents narrower than the pure fifth.

questions.explanation: Equal temperament sets the fifth at 700 cents. This is 2 cents narrower than the pure 702-cent fifth, enabling the circle to close.

questions.topic: A courtly genre and its subject
questions.stem: Ticket #158 explains courtly love; which option captures it?

options.text: Courtly love is physical desire between social equals.
Courtly love is marital duty within a household.

questions.topic: Counting the refrains across the formes fixe
questions.stem: Ticket #159 asks how many refrain returns a ballade with three stanzas and an envoy has.

answer.exemplar: A ballade with three stanzas and an envoy returns its refrain four times, once at the close of each stanza and the envoy.

questions.explanation: The refrain closes each of the three stanzas and the envoy, giving four returns. Counting stanzas alone gives three.
